texts.0: SP, due to a breakdown of the cross-check between control instruments, performance instruments and the outside visual cues, stopped correlating aircraft position with the assigned area and lost orientation during the maneuvering sequence. Altitude, heading and airspeed trends were left unmonitored and were not correlated with the aircraft position at any point. The aircraft left the assigned working area and descended through the briefed floor, and the IP had to take control to reposition it. The remaining profile was terminated.
texts.1: SP, due to a slow and incomplete cross-check of the control and performance instruments against the outside references, did not detect the developing deviation as a trend. Orientation relative to the field and to the area boundary was re-established only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. The correction was applied late and the resulting excursion reached the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that narrowed onto the outside references while maneuvering, delayed detection of a developing altitude and heading trend. SP recognized the deviation without prompting, restored the full scan and re-established orientation with respect to the field and the area. The excursion remained short of the standard limit and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of the control and performance instruments against the outside visual cues and kept accurate orientation with respect to the field, the assigned area and other traffic. Deviations were identified as trends and corrected promptly, with tasks prioritized correctly throughout the maneuvering.
texts.4: SP kept an uninterrupted scan across control instruments, performance instruments and outside references and continuously correlated aircraft position, fuel state and traffic. Trends were recognized before they developed into deviations, so corrections were minimal and the aircraft state stayed on the briefed parameters throughout the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP kept orientation and held the aircraft within the required standards, but the cross-check narrowed noticeably each time task loading increased and corrections were reactive rather than anticipatory. The trend was toward detecting deviations only after they were established. SP is expected to widen the scan under load and to act on the trend rather than on the deviation.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the cross-check between control and performance instruments and the outside cues inside the code 1 band, one developing trend held unmonitored for a short interval before orientation was reestablished. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to widen the scan under load so a trend is caught before it needs a larger correction.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the cross-check between control and performance instruments and the outside cues inside the code 2 band, correcting a scan that had narrowed onto the outside references while maneuvering. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to notice the narrowing a little sooner so the correction stays smaller.
texts_at.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of the control and performance instruments against the outside visual cues, correcting deviations as trends with only one brief narrowing of the scan during a demanding maneuver. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to hold that scan open through that maneuver as well.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the cross-check narrowing onto the outside references and restored the full scan without prompting, re-establishing orientation with respect to the field and the area. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good instrument and outside cross-check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of the control and performance instruments against the outside visual cues and kept accurate orientation with respect to the field, the assigned area and other traffic, identifying deviations as trends and correcting them promptly. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good instrument and outside cross-check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP kept an uninterrupted scan across control instruments, performance instruments and outside references, continuously correlating aircraft position, fuel state and traffic so trends were recognized before they became deviations. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent instrument and outside cross-check discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to a decision taken before gathering the available weather, fuel and traffic data, did not identify the contingency or state any alternative, and continued the profile past the briefed decision point. The developing hazard was neither recognized nor avoided and no rationale for the decision was provided when asked. The IP had to direct the deconfliction and the RTB.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete gathering of the available data before deciding, selected a course of action that did not account for the deteriorating conditions in the area. The hazard was identified and the decision revised only after the IP verbally pointed out the relevant cues. The delayed change of plan left the aircraft at the limit of the acceptable margin.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial assessment that weighed the mission task above the developing weather and traffic picture, delayed the decision to change the working area. SP gathered the remaining data, stated the revised decision clearly with its rationale and repositioned without prompting. The margins to the hazard were preserved and no IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP identified contingencies and alternatives accurately, gathered all available data before deciding, stated each decision clearly and supported it with sound rationale. Actual and potential hazards were recognized early and the flight was regulated to avoid them positively.
texts.4: SP anticipated the contingencies before they materialized, weighed weather, fuel, traffic and aircraft limitations against the mission task, and announced each decision with a concise and complete rationale. Hazards were avoided with wide margins and without any reduction in mission effectiveness.
texts.marginal: SP reached correct decisions and kept the flight clear of hazards, but the decisions were made close to the briefed decision points and the supporting rationale was thin when the IP asked for it. The trend was toward reacting to the situation rather than anticipating it. SP is expected to decide earlier and to articulate the reasoning behind each decision.

texts_at.1: SP identified contingencies and gathered the available data before deciding inside the code 1 band, one hazard identified and the decision revised only after it was pointed out. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to decide earlier and articulate the reasoning behind each decision without waiting to be asked.
texts_at.2: SP identified contingencies and gathered the available data before deciding inside the code 2 band, correcting a decision that had initially weighed the mission task above the developing weather picture. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to weigh the developing picture against the task a little earlier in the assessment.
texts_at.3: SP identified contingencies and alternatives accurately, gathered available data before deciding and stated each decision with sound rationale, with one decision reached slightly later in the sequence than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to reach that decision as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP gathered the remaining data unaided, stated a revised decision clearly with its rationale and repositioned without prompting, preserving the margins to the hazard. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound risk-based decision making.
texts_above.3: SP identified contingencies and alternatives accurately, gathered all available data before deciding, stated each decision clearly and supported it with sound rationale, recognizing hazards early and regulating the flight to avoid them positively. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed risk-based decision making.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the contingencies before they materialized, weighed weather, fuel, traffic and aircraft limitations against the mission task, and announced each decision with a concise and complete rationale, avoiding hazards with wide margins. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional risk-based decision making.

texts.0: SP, due to attention captured entirely by one minor cockpit indication, dropped every other task in the sequence and stopped flying the aircraft to the briefed parameters. Checklist steps, radio calls and lookout were all suspended while SP worked that single item, and a significant step was missed. The IP had to take control to restore the flight path and re-establish the task sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to channelized attention on the item being worked, handled the tasks one at a time and let the aircraft state and the radio go unattended. The omitted items were picked up only after the IP prompted verbally, and the sequence was restored late. Aircraft parameters reached the limit of the acceptable standard before the scan was resumed.
texts.2: SP, due to a fixation on one cockpit task while task loading was high, allowed the ordering of the remaining actions to slip. SP recognized the saturation, released the secondary task, returned to flying the aircraft first and completed the sequence without missing any significant item. Parameters stayed inside the standard and no IP prompting was required.
texts.3: SP ordered the tasks correctly by significance, handled several tasks in sequence without dropping any of them and violated no rule of the procedure. Aircraft control retained first priority throughout, and no sign of channelized attention was observed.
texts.4: SP sequenced every task by significance without hesitation, absorbed the added workload without any degradation of aircraft control, and kept spare capacity available for the radio and the lookout. Nothing significant was deferred or omitted at any point in the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP kept the correct order of tasks and missed nothing significant, but the sequence slowed markedly whenever two tasks arrived together and aircraft parameters drifted while the secondary task was worked. The trend was toward serial rather than parallel task handling. SP is expected to shed or defer secondary tasks earlier so that aircraft control retains first priority.

texts_at.1: SP ordered tasks by significance inside the code 1 band, one omitted item picked up only after it was prompted before the sequence was restored. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to shed or defer secondary tasks earlier so aircraft control retains first priority without prompting.
texts_at.2: SP ordered tasks by significance inside the code 2 band, correcting an ordering that had slipped while task loading was high on one occasion. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the saturation a little sooner so fewer items slip before the correction.
texts_at.3: SP ordered the tasks correctly by significance and handled several tasks in sequence without dropping any of them, with only one brief slip in pace when two tasks arrived together. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to hold that pace through the next such moment as well.

texts_above.2: SP recognized approaching saturation on one occasion, released the secondary task and returned to flying the aircraft first, completing the sequence without missing any significant item. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady task prioritization under load.
texts_above.3: SP ordered tasks correctly by significance, handled several tasks in sequence without dropping any of them and violated no rule of the procedure, keeping aircraft control first priority throughout with no sign of channelized attention. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate task prioritization under load.
texts_above.4: SP sequenced every task by significance without hesitation, absorbing added workload without any degradation of aircraft control and keeping spare capacity available for the radio and the lookout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary task prioritization under load.

error_modes.label: FLEXIBILITY AND MISSION ADJUSTMENT (TIME, FUEL, AREA)

texts.0: SP, due to rigid adherence to the briefed sequence of maneuvers, did not adjust the profile to the remaining flight time, the fuel state or the boundaries of the assigned area. Changing weather in the area was not assessed and no alternative course of action was selected. The IP had to direct the change of profile and the return to base with the fuel margin already reduced to the minimum.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect assessment of the factors bearing on the situation, kept the original profile after the conditions in the area had changed and did not foresee the effect on fuel and time. The profile was modified only after the IP stated the remaining fuel and the time available. The adjustment came late and the sortie was completed at the limit of the planned fuel reserve.
texts.2: SP, due to a late reassessment of the remaining flight time against the maneuvers still to be flown, initially planned a sequence that did not fit the fuel available. SP reassessed the factors without prompting, re-ordered the remaining maneuvers and selected a course of action that used the remaining fuel and area efficiently. The reserve and the area limits were respected throughout.
texts.3: SP assessed the factors bearing on the situation correctly and selected the best course of action, adjusting the execution of the mission to the available flight time, the fuel remaining, the weather and the assigned area. Alternative choices were made when needed and mission effectiveness was maintained.
texts.4: SP adapted to the changing conditions immediately and reordered the profile so that the remaining fuel, time and airspace were used to the maximum advantage. The outcome of each change was foreseen accurately and all briefed objectives were obtained without any reduction of the safety margins.
texts.marginal: SP adjusted the profile appropriately and completed the objectives within the available fuel, time and area, but the reassessment followed the change of conditions rather than anticipating it and the alternatives were considered only when the original plan no longer worked. The trend was toward late replanning. SP is expected to evaluate the remaining fuel, time and area continuously and to reshape the profile before the constraint becomes limiting.

texts_at.1: SP adjusted the profile to the available flight time, fuel state and assigned area inside the code 1 band, one effect on fuel and time foreseen only after it was pointed out. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to evaluate the remaining fuel, time and area continuously and reshape the profile before the constraint becomes limiting.
texts_at.2: SP adjusted the profile to the available flight time, fuel state and assigned area inside the code 2 band, correcting a sequence that had not initially fit the fuel available. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to reassess the remaining time against the maneuvers still to be flown a little earlier.
texts_at.3: SP assessed the factors bearing on the situation correctly and selected the best course of action, adjusting the mission to the available flight time, fuel and area with only one adjustment made a little later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to make that adjustment as promptly as the rest.

texts_above.2: SP reassessed the factors bearing on the situation without prompting, re-ordered the remaining maneuvers and selected a course of action that used the remaining fuel and area efficiently. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable mission adjustment to fuel, time and area.
texts_above.3: SP assessed the factors bearing on the situation correctly and selected the best course of action, adjusting the execution of the mission to the available flight time, fuel remaining, weather and assigned area while maintaining mission effectiveness. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good mission adjustment to fuel, time and area.
texts_above.4: SP adapted to the changing conditions immediately and reordered the profile so the remaining fuel, time and airspace were used to maximum advantage, foreseeing the outcome of each change accurately. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior mission adjustment to fuel, time and area.

error_modes.label: CAPACITY AND USE OF AVAILABLE RESOURCES

texts.0: SP, due to reluctance to state that the task loading had become unmanageable, continued the profile well past the point of saturation and did not select any alternative to reduce the workload. Aircraft control degraded, the required actions became disordered and no request for assistance or repetition was made. The IP had to take control and terminate the maneuver to restore a safe aircraft state.
texts.1: SP, due to unwillingness to declare saturation to the IP, accepted a task loading beyond the level that could be handled and let performance degrade before acting. The reduction of task loading was made only after the IP offered it explicitly. Aircraft parameters reached the limit of the acceptable standard before the workload was brought back under control.
texts.2: SP, due to a hesitation to state that the workload was becoming excessive, absorbed the additional tasks longer than appropriate. SP then recognized the approaching saturation, asked for the repetition to be delayed and reduced the task loading without waiting for the IP. Aircraft control and the required standards were preserved throughout.
texts.3: SP remained aware of the task loading that could be handled safely and never exceeded the capability to control the aircraft. When required, SP selected an alternative course of action to reduce the workload and stated it clearly, so that the mission was accomplished effectively.
texts.4: SP handled a high and increasing task loading without any sign of saturation, confusion or degradation of aircraft control, and retained spare capacity for the unbriefed items introduced during the sortie. Requests to adjust the workload, where useful, were made early, clearly and without hesitation.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the capability to control the aircraft safely and completed the mission, but signs of approaching saturation appeared under added task loading and the request to reduce it came only when performance was already degrading. The trend was toward absorbing workload silently. SP is expected to recognize the capacity limit earlier and to state it to the IP without hesitation.

texts_at.1: SP stayed aware of the task loading that could be handled safely inside the code 1 band, the reduction of task loading made only after it was offered before capacity was restored. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to recognize the capacity limit earlier and state it to the IP without hesitation.
texts_at.2: SP stayed aware of the task loading that could be handled safely inside the code 2 band, correcting an absorption of added tasks that had run a little longer than appropriate. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the approaching saturation a little sooner so less is absorbed before the correction.
texts_at.3: SP remained aware of the task loading that could be handled safely and never exceeded the capability to control the aircraft, selecting an alternative course of action when required with only one request voiced a little later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to voice that request as promptly as the rest.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the approaching saturation and asked for the repetition to be delayed, reducing the task loading without waiting for the IP and preserving aircraft control throughout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured workload capacity management.
texts_above.3: SP remained aware of the task loading that could be handled safely and never exceeded the capability to control the aircraft, selecting an alternative course of action when required and stating it clearly so the mission was accomplished effectively. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise workload capacity management.
texts_above.4: SP handled a high and increasing task loading without any sign of saturation, confusion or degradation of aircraft control, retaining spare capacity for the unbriefed items introduced during the sortie. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate workload capacity management.

error_modes.label: FLIGHT DISCIPLINE, CHECKS AND SOP COMPLIANCE

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the applicable rules and procedures, did not perform the operational checks in accordance with the Checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. Required steps were omitted and others were carried out in the wrong order, so the aircraft was operated outside the published configuration for that phase. The IP had to direct the missing actions and correct the configuration.
texts.1: SP, due to imprecise recall of the checklist sequence, carried out the operational checks incompletely and in a disordered manner. The omitted steps were completed only after verbal reminders from the IP at each occurrence. Continuous IP supervision was required for the procedures to be carried out to the published standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried start of the check sequence, initially performed the operational checks out of the published order. SP identified the discrepancy, restarted the affected part of the checklist and completed all required steps in accordance with the Checklist and the SOPs. No IP prompting was necessary and the aircraft configuration remained correct for the phase of flight.
texts.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the Checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs, carrying out every required step in the proper order. Knowledge of the applicable rules and regulations was complete and all duties were performed with minimum IP supervision.
texts.4: SP executed every check and procedure precisely and in the correct order, without omission and without reference prompts, and applied the governing rules correctly to each situation encountered. All duties were carried out independently, and the IP supervision required was limited to the safety observation role.
texts.marginal: SP completed all required checks in the proper order and complied with the applicable rules, but the flow was slow and depended on the written checklist at points where recall was expected, and one step needed a second look before it was confirmed. The trend was toward procedural compliance achieved through deliberate effort rather than habit. SP is expected to consolidate the checklist flow so that the procedures are carried out with minimum IP supervision.

texts_at.1: SP performed the operational checks in accordance with the Checklist and the SOPs inside the code 1 band, the affected part of the sequence restarted after a step had been performed out of order. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to consolidate the checklist flow so the procedures are carried out with minimum IP supervision.
texts_at.2: SP performed the operational checks in accordance with the Checklist and the SOPs inside the code 2 band, correcting a check sequence initially performed out of the published order. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to notice the discrepancy a little sooner so fewer steps need restarting.
texts_at.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the Checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs, carrying out every required step in the proper order with only one step needing a second look before it was confirmed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to confirm that step on the first look as well.

texts_above.2: SP identified a discrepancy in the check sequence and restarted the affected part unaided, completing all required steps in accordance with the Checklist and the SOPs. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent checklist and SOP compliance.
texts_above.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the Checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs, carrying out every required step in the proper order with complete knowledge of the applicable rules and minimum IP supervision. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined checklist and SOP compliance.
texts_above.4: SP executed every check and procedure precisely and in the correct order, without omission and without reference prompts, applying the governing rules correctly with IP supervision limited to the safety observation role. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless checklist and SOP compliance.

error_modes.label: CLEARING THE AIRSPACE WHILE ASSESSING A MALFUNCTION OR CONVERGING TRAFFIC

texts.0: SP, due to fixation on an unexpected converging A/C during a critical phase of flight, stopped clearing the airspace and stopped monitoring the A/C systems for the remainder of the maneuver. The dynamic picture of self and A/C relative to the traffic was not reassessed and no avoidance action was initiated. The IP had to take control, turn the aircraft away from the conflicting traffic and re-establish the clearing pattern. The remaining maneuvers were terminated.
texts.1: SP, due to the distraction produced by a caution indication during a critical phase of flight, interrupted the clearing scan and did not resume it while the malfunction was being assessed. Lookout and the systems monitoring were restored only after repeated verbal direction from the IP. The converging traffic was acquired late and the separation obtained was at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to attention drawn to an unexpected A/C in the working area, briefly interrupted the monitoring of the A/C systems while maneuvering. SP recognized the narrowing of attention without prompting, resumed the full clearing scan and completed the systems check. The traffic was deconflicted well before it became a factor and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP cleared the airspace continuously and monitored the A/C systems throughout, and did not allow the malfunction indication or the converging traffic to become a distraction during the critical phase of flight. Perception of self and A/C relative to the traffic, the environment and the mission was maintained, and the avoidance action was initiated in good time.
texts.4: SP maintained an aggressive clearing scan and continuous systems monitoring, acquired the converging A/C long before it became a factor and folded the assessment of the abnormal indication into the flow without any interruption of the lookout. Avoidance was accomplished with wide separation and the briefed sequence continued without degradation.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspace cleared and the systems monitored within the required standard, but the scan contracted noticeably each time an unexpected indication or an outside distraction appeared, and clearing resumed only once the distraction had been resolved. The trend was toward handling lookout and systems assessment in series rather than in parallel. SP is expected to keep the clearing scan running while any malfunction or traffic situation is being evaluated.

texts_at.1: SP cleared the airspace while assessing a malfunction or converging traffic inside the code 1 band, lookout and systems monitoring restored only after they were prompted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep the clearing scan running while any malfunction or traffic situation is being evaluated.
texts_at.2: SP cleared the airspace while assessing a malfunction or converging traffic inside the code 2 band, correcting a brief narrowing of attention onto an unexpected aircraft in the working area. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize that narrowing a little sooner so less of the scan is lost.
texts_at.3: SP cleared the airspace continuously and monitored the A/C systems throughout, not allowing the malfunction indication or the converging traffic to become a distraction during the critical phase of flight, with only a brief interruption of the systems check on one occasion. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to protect that check as well.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the narrowing of attention onto an unexpected aircraft without prompting, resumed the full clearing scan and completed the systems check with the traffic deconflicted well before it became a factor. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good clearing while assessing a malfunction.
texts_above.3: SP cleared the airspace continuously and monitored the A/C systems throughout, not allowing the malfunction indication or the converging traffic to become a distraction during the critical phase of flight, with perception of self and A/C relative to the traffic maintained and avoidance initiated in good time. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good clearing while assessing a malfunction.
texts_above.4: SP maintained an aggressive clearing scan and continuous systems monitoring, acquiring the converging aircraft long before it became a factor and folding the assessment of the abnormal indication into the flow without any interruption of the lookout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent clearing while assessing a malfunction.

error_modes.label: EMERGENCY RECOVERY PLAN ESTABLISHED BEFORE THE EMERGENCY

texts.0: SP, due to failure to establish an emergency recovery plan before an emergency occurred, had no nearest suitable field, no recovery heading and no energy assessment available when the simulated malfunction was introduced. The response was improvised, the aircraft was turned away from the closest recovery option and the fuel and altitude available were not used to advantage. The IP had to take control, state the recovery plan and direct the return to base.
texts.1: SP, due to an emergency recovery plan that was set up before departure and never updated as the working area changed, could not state the nearest suitable field or the recovery heading when the malfunction was introduced. The plan was reconstructed only after the IP prompted for it item by item. The recovery was initiated late and the energy margin available on reaching the field was at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed update of the recovery plan after repositioning within the area, initially referenced a field that was no longer the closest option. SP recognized the discrepancy without prompting, restated the nearest suitable field and the recovery heading, and turned toward it while completing the required actions. The recovery was flown with an adequate energy margin and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP established an emergency recovery plan before it was needed and maintained it throughout, keeping the nearest suitable field, the recovery heading and the energy available continuously in mind as the aircraft repositioned. When the malfunction was introduced the plan was executed immediately and the recovery was completed without hesitation.
texts.4: SP updated the emergency recovery plan at every change of area, altitude and fuel state, and stated it proactively so that it was current at all times. The malfunction was met with an immediate, pre-considered response, the aircraft was turned toward the best available field at once and the recovery was completed with a comfortable energy and fuel margin.
texts.marginal: SP was able to state a valid recovery plan and executed it correctly, but the plan lagged behind the aircraft position and was refreshed only when the profile changed rather than continuously. The trend was toward reconstructing the plan after the event instead of holding it ready. SP is expected to keep the nearest suitable field, recovery heading and energy state current at all times before an emergency occurs.

texts_at.1: SP established an emergency recovery plan before the emergency inside the code 1 band, the plan reconstructed item by item only after it was prompted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep the nearest suitable field, recovery heading and energy state current at all times before an emergency occurs.
texts_at.2: SP established an emergency recovery plan before the emergency inside the code 2 band, correcting a plan that had initially referenced a field no longer the closest option. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to update the plan at the moment the area changes rather than after it has changed.
texts_at.3: SP established an emergency recovery plan before it was needed and maintained it as the aircraft repositioned, executing it immediately without hesitation when the malfunction was introduced, with one update following the repositioning a little later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to make that update as promptly as the rest.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a delayed update of the recovery plan and restated the nearest suitable field and heading without prompting, turning toward it while completing the required actions. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound emergency recovery planning.
texts_above.3: SP established an emergency recovery plan before it was needed and maintained it throughout, keeping the nearest suitable field, the recovery heading and the energy available continuously in mind, executing the plan immediately when the malfunction was introduced. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed emergency recovery planning.
texts_above.4: SP updated the emergency recovery plan at every change of area, altitude and fuel state, stating it proactively so it was current at all times and met the malfunction with an immediate, pre-considered response. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional emergency recovery planning.

error_modes.label: INTERRUPTED CHECKLIST NOT RESTARTED AT THE CORRECT POINT

texts.0: SP, due to resuming an interrupted checklist from the point of recall instead of restarting at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, omitted a checklist item and did not positively confirm completion. A new checklist was then started before the previous one had been completed, so the omission was never detected. The aircraft was operated in a configuration not authorized for that phase of flight and the IP had to direct the missing actions.
texts.1: SP, due to picking the checklist back up one step after the interruption rather than two to three steps prior to it, left an item unconfirmed and did not verify completion of the checklist as a whole. The omission was identified and corrected only after a verbal reminder from the IP. The configuration was restored, but the delay left the aircraft at the limit of the acceptable standard for that phase.
texts.2: SP, due to a radio call that interrupted the checklist flow, initially resumed at the wrong point in the sequence. SP recognized the break, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step and positively confirmed completion before starting the next checklist. No item was omitted and no IP prompting was required.
texts.3: SP attempted every checklist without interruption and, when an interruption occurred, restarted at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step. Completion of each checklist was positively confirmed and no new checklist was started before the previous one had been completed.
texts.4: SP protected each checklist from interruption by sequencing the other cockpit tasks around it, and on the one occasion an interruption could not be avoided restarted well before the affected step and verified the whole sequence afterwards. Every checklist was positively confirmed complete, in order, with no omissions and without any reference prompt.
texts.marginal: SP completed all checklists and confirmed them, but after each interruption the resumption point was chosen by memory and the back-up steps were taken only after a visible pause for thought. The trend was toward relying on recall of where the flow was broken rather than on the published restart technique. SP is expected to restart at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step as a matter of habit.

texts_at.1: SP restarted an interrupted checklist at the correct point inside the code 1 band, an item left unconfirmed until it was pointed out. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to restart at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step as a matter of habit.
texts_at.2: SP restarted an interrupted checklist at the correct point inside the code 2 band, correcting a resumption initially made at the wrong point in the sequence. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the break in the flow a little sooner so the restart point is chosen correctly the first time.
texts_at.3: SP attempted every checklist without interruption and, when an interruption occurred, restarted at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, with one restart point chosen a little late in the recall. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to choose that point as promptly as the rest.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a break in the checklist flow, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step and positively confirmed completion before starting the next checklist, with no item omitted. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady checklist restart discipline.
texts_above.3: SP attempted every checklist without interruption and, when an interruption occurred, restarted at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, positively confirming completion of each checklist before starting the next. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate checklist restart discipline.
texts_above.4: SP protected each checklist from interruption by sequencing other cockpit tasks around it, and on the one occasion an interruption could not be avoided restarted well before the affected step and verified the whole sequence afterward. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary checklist restart discipline.

error_modes.label: OPERATIONS CHECK INTERVAL AND FENCE IN/OUT DISCIPLINE

texts.0: SP, due to concentrating exclusively on the maneuver sequence during area work, did not perform the operations check at any point and entered and left the MOA without a FENCE check. Fuel quantity and balance, engine indications, NAVAIDS and equipment were therefore never verified during the working period. The IP had to direct the checks and the aircraft state was found outside the briefed fuel and configuration expectations.
texts.1: SP, due to a loss of time awareness while maneuvering, allowed the interval between operations checks to stretch to more than double the fifteen minute standard and omitted the FENCE-out check on leaving the MOA. The checks were accomplished only after the IP called for them on each occasion. The engine and fuel state were confirmed acceptable but only at the limit of the briefed margins.
texts.2: SP, due to sequencing several maneuvers without reference to the clock, let the operations check slip past the fifteen minute point. SP noticed the omission without prompting, completed the full check and thereafter used the quarter hour as the trigger for the following checks. The remaining checks were on time and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP performed the operations check approximately every fifteen minutes while accomplishing area work and completed a FENCE check on entering and again on leaving the MOA. Fuel, engine, NAVAIDS, communications and equipment were verified at each check and the checks were not repeated between maneuvers flown in a series.
texts.4: SP anchored the operations checks to the quarter hour and used the clock stopwatch so that no check was late, and the FENCE-in and FENCE-out checks were completed precisely at the MOA boundaries. Each check was accomplished without interrupting the flow of the profile and every deviation in fuel or engine indications would have been caught at its earliest point.
texts.marginal: SP accomplished the operations checks and both FENCE checks within the required standard, but the timing depended on remembering to look at the clock and one interval ran close to the fifteen minute limit before the check was started. The trend was toward checks triggered by a gap in the profile rather than by time. SP is expected to tie the operations check to the stopwatch or to the quarter hour so the interval is protected.

texts_at.1: SP performed the operations check and the FENCE checks on their intervals inside the code 1 band, the interval stretching well past the standard before the checks were accomplished on prompting. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to tie the operations check to the stopwatch or to the quarter hour so the interval is protected.
texts_at.2: SP performed the operations check and the FENCE checks on their intervals inside the code 2 band, correcting an interval that had slipped past the fifteen minute point before it was noticed unaided. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to reference the clock a little more often so the interval does not need catching up.
texts_at.3: SP performed the operations check approximately every fifteen minutes while accomplishing area work and completed a FENCE check on entering and again on leaving the MOA, with one check triggered by a gap in the profile rather than by time. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to trigger that check by time as well.

texts_above.2: SP noticed the operations check slipping past the fifteen minute point without prompting, completed the full check and used the quarter hour as the trigger for the checks that followed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable operations check and FENCE timing.
texts_above.3: SP performed the operations check approximately every fifteen minutes while accomplishing area work and completed a FENCE check on entering and again on leaving the MOA, verifying fuel, engine, NAVAIDS, communications and equipment at each one. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good operations check and FENCE timing.
texts_above.4: SP anchored the operations checks to the quarter hour and the stopwatch so no check was late, completing the FENCE-in and FENCE-out checks precisely at the MOA boundaries without interrupting the flow of the profile. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior operations check and FENCE timing.

error_modes.label: CLEF CHECK PRIOR TO STALLS, SPINS AND AEROBATICS

texts.0: SP, due to proceeding directly from the previous maneuver into the setup, did not accomplish the CLEF check before the stall and spin series. The area and the CWS panel were not cleared, loose items were left unstowed and the fuel balance was not verified, with the imbalance already beyond the fifty pound limit. The IP had to stop the setup, direct the check and reposition the aircraft before the maneuver could be attempted.
texts.1: SP, due to treating the CLEF items as covered by the earlier FENCE check, entered the aerobatic setup with the fuel balance unverified and the clearing turn incomplete. The check was accomplished item by item only after the IP called for it, and the imbalance was found approaching the fifty pound limit. The maneuver was flown to standard but only after the delay imposed by the late check.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed transition from the previous maneuver, began the entry setup before completing the CLEF items. SP recognized the omission without prompting, stopped the setup, cleared the area and the CWS panel, confirmed loose items stowed, engine within limits and fuel balance well inside the fifty pound limit before proceeding. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP accomplished the CLEF check before each stall, spin and aerobatic maneuver, clearing the area and the CWS panel, confirming loose items stowed, engine indications within limits and fuel balance within fifty pounds. The check was not repeated between maneuvers flown in a series, in accordance with the manual.
texts.4: SP completed the CLEF check smoothly ahead of every stalling, spinning and aerobatic sequence, keeping the fuel balance managed so that the imbalance stayed close to zero and clearing the area in a pattern that covered the full maneuvering airspace. The checks were integrated into the setup without any loss of position, energy or time.
texts.marginal: SP completed the CLEF check before each maneuver and the fuel imbalance stayed inside the fifty pound limit, but the items were recited quickly and the clearing turn was abbreviated when the maneuver had to be started before leaving the area. The trend was toward compressing the check under time pressure. SP is expected to keep the clearing and fuel balance items deliberate regardless of the time available.

texts_at.1: SP accomplished the CLEF check before the stall, spin and aerobatic series inside the code 1 band, the check completed item by item only after it was called for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep the clearing and fuel balance items deliberate regardless of the time available.
texts_at.2: SP accomplished the CLEF check before the stall, spin and aerobatic series inside the code 2 band, correcting an entry setup begun before the check was complete. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the omission a little sooner so the setup is stopped before it advances further.
texts_at.3: SP accomplished the CLEF check before each stall, spin and aerobatic maneuver, clearing the area and the CWS panel and confirming loose items, engine and fuel balance, with the clearing turn abbreviated once under time pressure. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to keep that turn to the same standard under pressure.

texts_above.2: SP recognized an entry setup begun before the CLEF items were complete, stopped the setup and completed the check before proceeding, with no IP intervention required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured CLEF check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP accomplished the CLEF check before each stall, spin and aerobatic maneuver, clearing the area and the CWS panel, confirming loose items stowed, engine indications within limits and fuel balance within the published margin, not repeating the check between maneuvers flown in series. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise CLEF check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP completed the CLEF check smoothly ahead of every stalling, spinning and aerobatic sequence, keeping the fuel imbalance close to zero and clearing the area in a pattern that covered the full maneuvering airspace. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate CLEF check discipline.

error_modes.label: JOKER AND BINGO FUEL AS DECISION GATES

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the regular fuel checks during the sortie, did not use the briefed joker fuel as the transition point and continued the profile past bingo fuel without initiating a recovery. The remaining sortie was flown with no assessment of the fuel required to reach the intended destination. The IP had to direct the recovery, and the aircraft returned with the reserve reduced below the planned figure.
texts.1: SP, due to infrequent fuel checks, passed the pre-planned joker fuel without transitioning to the next phase of the profile and recognized the bingo state only when the IP stated it. The recovery was initiated on IP direction and the aircraft arrived at the destination with the fuel at the minimum required figure. Continuous IP monitoring of the fuel state was necessary.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating on the maneuver sequence, allowed one fuel check to be missed and passed the joker fuel point unnoticed. SP detected the fuel state at the next check without prompting, terminated the current phase and initiated the recovery well before bingo fuel. The intended destination was reached with the planned reserve intact.
texts.3: SP performed regular fuel checks throughout the mission, used the briefed joker fuel as the trigger for the planned transition and initiated the recovery prior to reaching bingo fuel. The remaining profile was matched to the fuel available and the aircraft arrived at the intended destination with the required fuel.
texts.4: SP integrated the fuel check into every operations check, tracked the trend against the briefed joker and bingo figures and adjusted the sequence of the remaining maneuvers so that each objective was completed before its fuel gate. The recovery was initiated ahead of the plan and the aircraft landed with a comfortable margin above the required fuel.
texts.marginal: SP performed the fuel checks and respected the joker and bingo figures, but the checks were spaced unevenly and the transition at joker fuel followed the figure rather than anticipating it. The trend was toward reading the fuel state as a limit reached rather than as a planning tool. SP is expected to check fuel at regular intervals and to shape the remaining profile before the joker figure is reached.

texts_at.1: SP used the briefed joker and bingo fuel figures as decision gates inside the code 1 band, the bingo state recognized only after it was stated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to check fuel at regular intervals and shape the remaining profile before the joker figure is reached.
texts_at.2: SP used the briefed joker and bingo fuel figures as decision gates inside the code 2 band, correcting a missed fuel check that had let the joker point pass unnoticed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to space the fuel checks a little more evenly so none is missed.
texts_at.3: SP performed regular fuel checks throughout the mission, used the briefed joker fuel as the trigger for the planned transition and initiated the recovery prior to reaching bingo fuel, with one check spaced a little wider than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to space that check as evenly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP detected the fuel state at the next check without prompting after one earlier check was missed, terminating the current phase and initiating the recovery well before bingo fuel. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound use of joker and bingo fuel gates.
texts_above.3: SP performed regular fuel checks throughout the mission, used the briefed joker fuel as the trigger for the planned transition and initiated the recovery prior to reaching bingo fuel, matching the remaining profile to the fuel available. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed use of joker and bingo fuel gates.
texts_above.4: SP integrated the fuel check into every operations check, tracked the trend against the briefed joker and bingo figures and adjusted the sequence of the remaining maneuvers so each objective was completed before its fuel gate. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional use of joker and bingo fuel gates.

error_modes.label: GO-AROUND WHEN THE LANDING ATTEMPT LOOKS OR FEELS WRONG

texts.0: SP, due to an attempt to salvage a landing that was recognized as abnormal, continued the approach with the aircraft out of position and the pattern situation deteriorating instead of executing a go-around. The abnormal situation was not identified as one requiring an immediate go-around and no decision was stated. The IP had to take control and initiate the go-around from an unsafe position.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation to abandon a landing attempt that both looked and felt wrong, continued the approach and initiated the go-around only after the IP directed it. The recovery from the abnormal situation was correct once started, but the delay left the aircraft at the limit of the acceptable standard for the pattern.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial attempt to correct an approach that was developing abnormally, continued briefly before reassessing. SP recognized without prompting that the attempt could not be salvaged, stated the decision and executed a clean go-around from a safe position. Pattern spacing and the traffic situation were preserved and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the traffic pattern promptly and executed a go-around without hesitation when the landing attempt looked or felt wrong. When the location of other traffic was in doubt the tower controller was queried, and the pattern was rejoined in accordance with the published procedure.
texts.4: SP identified the developing abnormality early, stated the go-around decision before the situation degraded and flew the go-around and the re-entry to the pattern precisely, with the tower informed and the traffic picture clarified in advance. No attempt was made to salvage a compromised approach at any point in the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP executed the required go-arounds and kept the pattern within standards, but each decision was taken late in the approach after a period of trying to correct the situation. The trend was toward salvaging first and deciding afterwards. SP is expected to go around immediately when a landing attempt looks or simply feels wrong, without attempting to correct it first.

texts_at.1: SP recognized an abnormal landing attempt and executed a go-around inside the code 1 band, the go-around initiated only after it was directed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to go around immediately when a landing attempt looks or simply feels wrong, without attempting to correct it first.
texts_at.2: SP recognized an abnormal landing attempt and executed a go-around inside the code 2 band, correcting a brief continuation of the approach before reassessing. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to reassess the approach a little sooner so the continuation is shorter.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the traffic pattern promptly and executed a go-around without hesitation when the landing attempt looked or felt wrong, querying the tower when traffic location was in doubt, with one decision reached a little later in the approach than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to reach that decision as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized without prompting that a developing approach could not be salvaged, stated the decision and executed a clean go-around from a safe position with pattern spacing preserved. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good go-around judgment on a compromised landing.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the traffic pattern promptly and executed a go-around without hesitation when the landing attempt looked or felt wrong, querying the tower controller when the location of other traffic was in doubt and rejoining the pattern in accordance with the published procedure. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good go-around judgment on a compromised landing.
texts_above.4: SP identified the developing abnormality early, stated the go-around decision before the situation degraded and flew the go-around and re-entry to the pattern precisely, with the tower informed and the traffic picture clarified in advance. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent go-around judgment on a compromised landing.

error_modes.label: STALL INDICATIONS IN THE PATTERN - RECOVERY BEFORE GROUND TRACK

texts.0: SP, due to prioritizing the ground track over the aircraft state, continued to fly the pattern to the runway alignment after stall indications were observed and did not execute the stall recovery procedure. Bank and back stick pressure were maintained while the indications persisted, so the aircraft was flown deeper into the stall regime at low altitude. The IP had to take control, unload the aircraft and complete the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to accept the resulting displacement from the desired ground track, delayed the stall recovery after the indications appeared and applied only a partial unloading. The full recovery procedure was flown only after the IP directed it. The indications ceased and the pattern was continued, but the margin obtained was at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial attempt to hold the turn to final while the indications were developing, was slow to unload the aircraft. SP recognized the priority without prompting, executed the stall recovery procedure and disregarded the ground track until the aircraft was flying cleanly. The pattern was re-established from a safe position and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP recognized the stall indications immediately and executed the stall recovery procedure at once, disregarding the ground track as directed by the manual. Once the aircraft was clean, SP reassessed the position relative to the field and the traffic and either re-entered the pattern or went around as appropriate.
texts.4: SP flew the pattern with an energy margin that kept stall indications from developing, and on the one occasion an indication appeared the recovery was initiated instantly, with ground track disregarded and the aircraft unloaded before the condition could progress. The subsequent repositioning was accomplished without any effect on the traffic pattern flow.
texts.marginal: SP recovered correctly whenever stall indications appeared and stayed within the required standards, but the first response each time was a brief glance at the runway alignment before unloading the aircraft. The trend was toward weighing the ground track against the recovery. SP is expected to execute the stall recovery procedure and disregard ground track the moment any stall indication is observed.

texts_at.1: SP gave priority to the stall recovery over the ground track inside the code 1 band, the full recovery procedure flown only after it was directed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to execute the stall recovery procedure and disregard ground track the moment any stall indication is observed.
texts_at.2: SP gave priority to the stall recovery over the ground track inside the code 2 band, correcting an initial attempt to hold the turn to final while the indications were developing. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the priority a little sooner so less time passes before the aircraft is unloaded.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the stall indications immediately and executed the stall recovery procedure at once, disregarding the ground track as directed by the manual, with one reassessment of position following a little later than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to reach that reassessment as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the priority between holding the turn and the stall recovery without prompting, executed the recovery and disregarded the ground track until the aircraft was flying cleanly, with the pattern re-established from a safe position. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent priority given to the stall recovery in the pattern.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the stall indications immediately and executed the stall recovery procedure at once, disregarding the ground track as directed by the manual, and reassessed position relative to the field and the traffic once the aircraft was clean. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined priority given to the stall recovery in the pattern.
texts_above.4: SP flew the pattern with an energy margin that kept stall indications from developing, and on the one occasion an indication appeared the recovery was initiated instantly with ground track disregarded before the condition could progress. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless priority given to the stall recovery in the pattern.
